sections.html:
Naperville sits about 28 miles west of Chicago and spans two counties, DuPage and Will. Population is 153,114 as of July 1, 2025, and the typical owner-occupied home is worth $540,200. About 74.8% of homes are lived in by their owners, and the median household income is $155,105.

Housing ranges from older downtown properties to subdivision homes built in the 1980s and 1990s, and buyers and appraisers treat those two groups differently. The city also spreads across six townships. Winfield, Milton, Naperville and Lisle are on the DuPage side, and Wheatland and DuPage townships are on the Will side. Some pockets, such as the unincorporated Tamarack neighborhood in the southwest, are cut out of the city limits, so a Naperville mailing address does not always mean the property is inside the city. That matters because the city's transfer stamp applies only to incorporated property.

sections.h2: Which county records a Naperville deed?
sections.html:
It depends on which side of the county line the parcel is on. Your tax bill or your last recorded deed shows the county. DuPage parcels go to the DuPage County Recorder, and Will parcels go to the Will County Recorder of Deeds in Joliet.

The two offices charge different fees for the same kind of document. Fees can change, so ask the recorder for the current figure before closing.

Standard deed recording fees by county
RecorderStandard deed feeWhat it includes
DuPage County Recorder$86.00Recording, document storage ($10), GIS ($31), real property ($1) and Rental Housing Support Program ($18)
Will County Recorder of Deeds$90.00 (effective October 1, 2025)Includes a $19.00 Rental Housing Support Program surcharge, dropped for government filers

For questions about the state transfer declaration, call the Illinois Department of Revenue MyDec help line at 844-445-1114. On the Will side, a deed needs the preparer and return addresses, the permanent index number, a legal description, a notarized original deed, the grantee name and address, a tax bill name and address, and a completed transfer declaration or exemption.

sections.h2: How the Naperville transfer tax stamp works
sections.html:
The buyer of a residential or commercial property inside incorporated Naperville buys the transfer tax stamp. The rate is $1.50 per $500 of purchase price, rounded up to the next $500 step. The stamp applies only to incorporated property, and the city's Your Place application, under Planning/Zoning Info, shows whether an address is inside the limits. Naperville is also among the municipalities whose stamps must be on a deed recorded with Will County.

The city asks for three things:

  • A Statement of Open Account letter, requested online no later than seven business days before closing.
  • A sales contract, a PTAX (MyDec) form or a sheriff's receipt carrying both buyer and seller signatures.
  • A copy of the deed that will be recorded with the county.

Allow up to seven business days of processing, whether you apply online or drop a packet at the Finance Department. The Customer Care Center at 630-420-6059 answers questions Monday through Friday, 7 am to 7 pm. The open account statement has its own seven business day lead time, so a closing set only a week out leaves no slack.

An exempt stamp is for a deed change on property you already own, with no sale price involved. It costs nothing and covers properties inside the city limits only.

The city's examples:

  • Moving the property into or out of a trust.
  • A divorce, or removing a name.
  • A marriage, or adding a name.
  • A legal name change.
  • A refinance.
  • A foreclosure where the sheriff's deed puts the property in bank ownership. If an individual buys at the sheriff's sale, that buyer purchases a regular stamp.

The exempt packet needs the open account statement, a Certificate for Exemption (mailed and in-person applications only) and a copy of the notarized deed. If you are moving a house between names before a sale, start with this packet, and give yourself the same seven business day cushion.

Start with any work done after you bought the house. Naperville's permit list has separate entries for decks, patios and sheds, driveways, fences, generators, lawn sprinkler systems with an RPZ backflow preventer, plumbing, electrical work, swimming pools and residential room additions or alterations.

If you cannot find paperwork for a finished basement, a deck or a sprinkler system, call the city and ask whether a permit was issued for that address. Learn the answer before a buyer's inspector or attorney asks.

If the house has unfinished work you do not want to complete, a buyer paying cash can take it as it stands and handle permits afterward.

Flood history is the weather topic that affects a sale here. The area took 14 inches of rain in under 24 hours in 1996, DuPage County was declared a disaster area, and damage topped $30 million. A second major flood followed in 2013.

Much of the land along the West Branch of the DuPage River belongs to the Forest Preserve District, which keeps development out of the floodplain. Even so, ask your insurance agent about your parcel before you list, since buyers' lenders will ask about flood zones too. Average precipitation runs about 37.7 inches a year, so on older homes buyers look first at sump pumps, gutters and grading.

Naperville Community Unit District 203 serves central and northern Naperville, with Naperville Central and Naperville North high schools. Indian Prairie School District 204 serves much of the rest. Small areas fall in District 200 on the DuPage side, and Plainfield District 202 and Valley View District 365U on the Will side. Confirm the district for your address before you advertise.

Interstate 88 crosses the north end, and Illinois Route 59 meets it at a diverging diamond interchange. Metra and Amtrak both stop in Naperville on the BNSF line, and the average commute is 30.5 minutes each way.

sections.h2: Selling without repairs and getting ready for closing
sections.html:
You can sell a Naperville house as it is. Whether a buyer takes the property in present condition is a term of your contract, and the city side of the closing is the stamp packet and the statement of open accounts, neither of which asks for repairs.

A workable order of steps: confirm the county and whether the parcel is inside city limits, gather permit records, request the Statement of Open Account online, and collect the signed contract or PTAX form. Have the deed ready for the county recorder. A cash buyer usually accepts the house in its current state and works to your closing date, which suits a seller who wants to skip showings and repair lists.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Naperville house without fixing it up?
faqs.a: Yes. Whether a buyer takes the property in present condition is a term of your contract. The city side of the closing is the transfer stamp packet and the statement of open accounts, and neither asks you to make repairs first.

faqs.q: Who pays the Naperville transfer tax stamp?
faqs.a: The buyer does. The city ordinance requires buyers of residential or commercial property inside incorporated Naperville to buy the stamp, at $1.50 per $500 of purchase price.

faqs.q: How early should I start the Naperville paperwork before closing?
faqs.a: At least seven business days early. The Statement of Open Account request is due no later than seven business days before closing, and stamp processing can take up to seven business days.

faqs.q: Does it matter if my Naperville home is on the Will County side?
faqs.a: It changes where the deed is recorded and the fee. Will County's standard document fee is $90.00 from October 1, 2025, while DuPage County's is $86.00. The city's own stamp rules are the same on both sides.

faqs.q: Which deed changes in Naperville need an exempt stamp?
faqs.a: Any change of name on a house you already own, such as adding a spouse, removing a name after a divorce, moving the property into a trust or refinancing. A sheriff's deed that puts the property in bank ownership also qualifies, with no fee.
